title: A relay of monsoon winds, brokers, and letters from the Swahili coast to southern China
register: documentary, skeptical of the schematic map-line
summary: No ruler, company, or fleet owned this network: the monsoon reversed on a six-month clock, and a chain of brokers, customs houses, and merchant correspondence relayed gold, pepper, and porcelain between ports that rarely saw one ship sail the whole way from the Swahili coast to southern China. What held it together was reputation, duplicated letters, and the wind itself, not a treaty or an army. It did not end in 1511, when Portuguese carracks began requiring passes for water that had never needed one; it was forced into a new arena of forts and licenses, and most of its old brokers kept trading inside it.

nodes.name: Mogadishu
nodes.note: The Benadir coast's leading port, exporting cloth, ivory, and captives toward Arabia and western India. The record is built from Arabic geography, ceramics, and later Portuguese description rather than any surviving customs ledger.

nodes.name: Barawa
nodes.note: An intermediate Benadir port linking Somali hinterlands to the wider ocean; its rank relative to Mogadishu shifted over the centuries but the town itself is securely attested.

nodes.name: Shanga
nodes.note: An early urbanizing and Islamic node in the Lamu archipelago. Excavated mosque phases, houses, and imported ceramics and glass attest a trading town from perhaps the eighth century; its urban role faded by the fifteenth.

nodes.name: Manda
nodes.note: A northern Swahili transshipment and craft center on the Lamu archipelago, roughly 20–25 hectares at its height, with imported ceramics running around a tenth of the domestic pottery assemblage around 1100 — a frequency, not a trade-value share.

nodes.name: Mombasa
nodes.note: An anchorage and commercial town between the Lamu towns and Zanzibar, later a diplomatic and strategic center; Malindi's neighbor and rival on the same stretch of coast.

nodes.name: Malindi
nodes.note: A commercial town whose 1498 cooperation with Vasco da Gama's fleet made it the launching point for the Cape route's final leg into the ocean; its later reputation as the source of China's 1414 giraffe compresses a transfer that actually passed through Bengal.

nodes.name: Pemba, Tumbe
nodes.note: A substantial early settlement, roughly 600 to 950, with unusually dense imported goods for its size; a node of northern coastal redistribution, craft, fishing, and farming rather than a purely commercial outpost.

nodes.name: Zanzibar, Unguja Ukuu
nodes.note: A large pre-urban port active from the seventh to the mid-eleventh century, its middens holding Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Chinese ceramics alongside imported beads. Bead chemistry suggests it and its neighbor Fukuchani belonged to somewhat separate commercial circuits rather than one uniform coastal market.

nodes.name: Kilwa Kisiwani
nodes.note: The principal intermediary for gold moving from the Zimbabwe plateau through Sofala, and a major entrepôt in ivory, timber, textiles, and ceramics from the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries. Its coral-stone mosques and palace survive; its supposed monopoly over southeastern African trade is probably an exaggeration of what was, at most, first among rivals. A Portuguese fort in 1505 ended its independent commercial standing.

nodes.name: Sofala
nodes.note: The principal outlet for gold from the Zimbabwe plateau, reached from the interior by river, overland carriage, and regional markets rather than one road. A Portuguese fort imposed in 1505 subordinated it to a new fiscal regime.

nodes.name: Chibuene
nodes.note: The earlier southern entry point for imported beads and the interior gold trade, active roughly 700 to 1000 before Sofala took over that role.

nodes.name: Aden
nodes.note: The western Indian Ocean's best-documented brokerage and customs center, its furda, governors, brokers, and Jewish courts known mainly from Cairo Geniza letters — Princeton's continuing census counts 668 documents and rising, mostly dated 1080 to 1240. It connected Egypt, Red Sea Arabia, East Africa, Gujarat, and Malabar.

nodes.name: Jeddah
nodes.note: The principal maritime gateway for Mecca, carrying pilgrims, merchants, and high-value cargo up the Red Sea; reefs, difficult winds, and taxation shaped every approach.

nodes.name: ʿAydhab
nodes.note: An Egyptian Red Sea transit point linked to the Nile by desert caravan, one of the two main channels — with Jeddah — by which Indian Ocean goods reached Fustat and Alexandria.

nodes.name: Mecca
nodes.note: Simultaneously a pilgrimage destination, a market, and a legal-religious center; pilgrim shipping carried merchandise and merchants performed pilgrimage, categories the sources never separate cleanly.

nodes.name: Siraf
nodes.note: A Persian Gulf entrepôt serving Basra, Iran, India, and China at its ninth- and tenth-century peak, known mainly through archaeology and Arabic accounts. Earthquakes, political shifts, and channel changes dispersed its trade toward Kish and Hormuz rather than ending it at a stroke.

nodes.name: Kish
nodes.note: Rose after Siraf's decline as a Gulf entrepôt, and was in turn eclipsed by Hormuz.

nodes.name: Hormuz
nodes.note: The major thirteenth- through fifteenth-century interchange between Iran, Arabia, India, and routes farther east; in 1442 the Timurid envoy ʿAbd al-Razzāq described it as frequented by sailors from Bengal, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, and lands facing China — a statement of perceived reach, not a ship register. Portuguese operations targeted it from 1507 but did not take it within this network's bounds.

nodes.name: Dhofar
nodes.note: Supplied aromatics, water, and staging for ships crossing between South Arabia, the Horn, and India.

nodes.name: Shihr
nodes.note: A South Arabian coastal town providing water, transshipment, and pilots along the Aden–Gulf corridor.

nodes.name: Qalhat
nodes.note: An Omani way-station on the approach to the Gulf, its importance shifting with South Arabian and Omani political fortune.

nodes.name: Muscat
nodes.note: An Omani anchorage and staging port on the approach to Hormuz.

nodes.name: Socotra
nodes.note: An island astride routes linking Aden, the Horn of Africa, East Africa, and India, its control shifting among South Arabian powers.

nodes.name: Khambhat
nodes.note: Gujarat's major manufacturing and redistribution port, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, and beads and importing horses, metals, and East African goods; it linked the Persian Gulf, Red Sea, East Africa, and Southeast Asia.

nodes.name: Bharuch
nodes.note: One of Gujarat's estuarine feeder ports, its fortunes tied to silting and shifting channels; the recipient address of Khalaf ibn Ishāq's Aden account, sent here to Ḥalfon ben Netanʾel around 1134.

nodes.name: Diu
nodes.note: A Gujarati port whose fortunes were bound to Khambhat's shifting estuary; a 1509 Portuguese naval victory offshore broke the Egyptian–Gujarati coalition and reordered the western Indian coast's balance of power.

nodes.name: Chaul
nodes.note: A Konkan port connecting hinterland produce to ocean shipping; the site of a 1508 Egyptian–Gujarati victory over a Portuguese squadron, one of the network's few outright military successes against the newcomers.

nodes.name: Goa
nodes.note: A Konkan port taken by Afonso de Albuquerque in 1510, after which it became the seat of Portuguese power in the Indian Ocean rather than an independent node of the older network.

nodes.name: Mangalore
nodes.note: A Kanara port exceptionally visible because Abraham Ben Yijū, a Jewish merchant from the western Islamic world, lived and manufactured here in the 1130s and 1140s, corresponding with Aden. His surviving papers describe one merchant's network, not the whole port's commerce.

nodes.name: Calicut
nodes.note: The principal late-medieval Malabar entrepôt under the Samutiri (Zamorin), whose open-market policy and Muslim merchant leadership drew Gujarati, Arab, Persian, Chinese, and other trade regardless of origin; the pepper port da Gama reached in 1498.

nodes.name: Cochin
nodes.note: Rose in importance through the fifteenth century and allied with the Portuguese against its rival Calicut after 1500.

nodes.name: Kollam
nodes.note: An early and major Malabar port with ties to the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Sri Lanka, and China; ships bound for it were themselves called 'Kūlamī,' as in the vessel whose disappearance around 1134 produced one of the network's best-documented legal cases.

nodes.name: Mantai
nodes.note: A major early-medieval transshipment center between the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, its craft debris and imports from many regions excavated; its role faded as shorelines, kingdoms, and trade patterns shifted.

nodes.name: Satgaon
nodes.note: A Bengal port exporting textiles, rice, and sugar, and a Bay of Bengal terminus for inland river systems.

nodes.name: Chittagong
nodes.note: The other principal Bengal port, linking the Bay of Bengal to inland Bengal's rivers and produce.

nodes.name: Srivijaya, Palembang
nodes.note: From about the seventh century this polity profited from traffic through and around the Straits of Malacca, though claims of complete control over the strait overstate a fluctuating authority; alternative passages and piracy both persisted alongside it.

nodes.name: Kedah
nodes.note: A Malay Peninsula port collecting and redistributing forest products, spices, and metals; Tamil merchant-guild inscriptions attest its reach into South Indian commercial networks.

nodes.name: Aceh
nodes.note: A northern Sumatran provisioning and collecting port for the western approach to the Straits, its political allegiance and merchant residence changing frequently.

nodes.name: Malacca
nodes.note: Formed around 1400, though the exact date and the circumstances of its ruler's conversion to Islam are disputed traditions rather than settled fact. By the fifteenth century its shahbandars, warehouses, and multilingual brokerage made it the transshipment hub between the Bay of Bengal, the Indonesian archipelago, and the South China Sea, ending as an independent node when Afonso de Albuquerque took it in August 1511.

nodes.name: Guangzhou
nodes.note: A major Tang and Song maritime port with a foreign quarter, its own headman, and maritime-trade supervision; Huang Chao's rebels killed foreign merchants here in 878–879, though the huge death tolls later Arabic reports give are not reliable counts.

nodes.name: Quanzhou
nodes.note: Known to Arabic and western accounts as Zaytūn, this became the Song and Yuan dynasties' greatest maritime-trade port after its Maritime Trade Office opened in 1087; Zhao Rukuo compiled the Zhufan zhi here in 1225. The office's transfer to Fuzhou in 1472 marked the end of its formal supervisory role.

nodes.name: Fustat, Cairo
nodes.note: Not itself an Indian Ocean port but the crucial terminus where Red Sea cargo, arriving by desert and river, met the Mediterranean; the Ben Ezra Synagogue's Geniza preserved letters that had traveled here from India and Aden, and its rabbinic courts sometimes ruled on Indian Ocean cases referred from Aden.

nodes.name: Abraham Ben Yijū
nodes.note: A Jewish merchant from the western Islamic world who resided at Mangalore from about 1132, ran a brass workshop, and corresponded with Aden. He owned an enslaved agent, Bomma, who conducted business in Aden on his behalf — commercial agency that must not be mistaken for partnership, since Bomma remained legally owned throughout.

nodes.name: The Aden India-traders circle
nodes.note: A working name for Maḍmūn ibn Ḥasan ibn Bundār, Aden's merchant leader and Ben Yijū's correspondent; his agent Khalaf ibn Ishāq, whose circa-1134 account to Ḥalfon ben Netanʾel in Bharuch is the only surviving full-year Aden-to-India summary, totaling 1,469 dinars, mostly pepper and textiles; and Ḥalfon himself, a merchant-scholar who traveled among Egypt, Aden, and India. Their documentary visibility comes from Geniza preservation, not necessarily from commercial dominance over Aden's wider, multi-confessional merchant society.

nodes.name: The Ainnurruvar (Five Hundred) merchant guild
nodes.note: The Ainnurruvar or Ayyavole Five Hundred, attested in Tamil inscriptions alongside associations such as the Manigramam and Anjuvannam, endowed temples, negotiated trading privileges, and organized protection across the Coromandel coast and beyond; they were not a unified corporation, and their organization varied by time and place.

nodes.name: Zhao Rukuo
nodes.note: A Chinese maritime-trade official at Quanzhou who compiled the Zhufan zhi in 1225, describing foreign countries and commodities from both documentary material and merchants' testimony. He did not personally visit most of the places he described.

nodes.name: Aḥmad ibn Mājid
nodes.note: A fifteenth-century Arab navigator whose Kitāb al-fawāʾid systematized winds, stellar navigation, routes, and port approaches. The persistent story that he personally piloted Vasco da Gama from Malindi to Calicut in 1498 is disputed and probably a later identification; near-contemporary Portuguese sources do not securely name him.

nodes.name: The monsoon wind system
nodes.note: The seasonal reversal of winds over the Arabian Sea and adjoining waters — broadly southwesterly from June through September or October, northeasterly from November through April or May — that made long open-water passages schedulable without making them safe. It is the one constant tying every other node in this network together, and the reason a China–Arabia round trip could take about two years.

nodes.name: The Aden furḍa
nodes.note: Aden's customs house, which controlled anchorage space, weighing, and clearance; a circa-1135 letter from Maḍmūn to Ben Yijū itemizes customs, freight, porterage, and safekeeping charges layered onto the price of copper and pepper passing through it.

nodes.name: The Sofala–Kilwa gold corridor
nodes.region: Zimbabwe plateau to Sofala and Kilwa
nodes.note: The chain of producers, chiefs, caravan organizers, and coastal merchants carrying gold from Zimbabwe-plateau polities to the coast, mainly through Sofala and thence through Kilwa. No evidence supports foreign merchants traveling freely inland to the mines themselves; the corridor's coastal end, not its interior, is what the record actually documents.

nodes.name: The Ming treasure fleets
nodes.note: Seven expeditions under Zheng He, 1405–1433, connected China with Southeast Asia, India, Sri Lanka, Hormuz, Arabia, and East Africa, combining diplomacy, tribute collection, trade, and naval intervention along lanes and using ports the fleets did not create. Often-repeated totals of over 300 ships and 27,000 to 37,000 personnel depend on how expeditionary and support vessels are counted.

nodes.name: The Portuguese cartaz system
nodes.note: A naval pass imposed from 1502 specifying a ship's vessel, route, and cargo; ships sailing without one risked seizure. It functioned simultaneously as licensing, surveillance, customs enforcement, and a means of sorting allies from targets, and was evaded, forged, or sailed around about as often as it was obeyed.

nodes.name: The Estado da Índia
nodes.note: The Portuguese crown's Indian Ocean administration, built from 1505 onward on captured or built forts, factories, and customs stations layered onto existing anchorages, brokers, and pilots. It could seize chokepoints more readily than it could control every coastal voyage, and most of the older network's merchants kept trading around, under, or despite it.
